title: How do you keep a games soul that is 100% vibe coded
author: Plus_Combination_553
selftext:
I am starting to create my own games. I always had ideas but I was never able to implement them.

With ai I started to create my own mobile games.  
Now I wonder what your opinion on ai generated games is. Is it more valuable when it comes from a human hand, instead of vibe code?

Do you think you can differ between ai generated and human genereated work?

comments.author: gardens_and_dungeons
comments.body: You create your vision, you are the lead. Just because it uses ai doesn't mean it's not your vision. Remember non ai games lack soul as well like yearly fifa releases.

replies.author: Plus_Combination_553
replies.body: Exactly. The soul comes from who makes the decisions, not from the tool. If you decide what the game should feel like, the AI is just a faster pencil. And the FIFA example proves it: plenty of fully handmade games are made without anyone caring.

comments.author: Vegetable_Voice_2044
comments.body:
Ai is a tool as much as a table saw is. I don't judge a house as being less valuable just because the craftsman didn't use a handsaw for every board. Just as I do not judge the developer for using ai to create their video game.

Both are capable of doing great work, both are capable of doing lazy work. The product speaks for itself.

replies.author: Plus_Combination_553
replies.body: I wonder why so many people are dissapointed when they learn a game is implemented with ai

replies.author: Vegetable_Voice_2044
replies.body:
There is a moral aspect that many feel that ai is the greatest theft of labor in human history. And that using ai means to support that theft. But the reality many of us have accepted is that AI is here to stay regardless of how it was trained... It's never going away, and what was done cannot be undone.
Regulations should be a thing, but I'm not going to avoid the tool because of how immoral it's creator was about making it.

replies.author: Xanma_6aki
replies.body: I think because people see it as lazy and lack of effort, which is fair enough

replies.author: acexprt
replies.body: It’s a moral thing at this point. Data centers, environment. Same reason people hated on crypto. The thing is, AI is being adopted massively and there is no getting away from it now.

comments.author: Bananaskovitch
comments.body: Doing drafts for a lot of things and iterating until it matches your vision. That's it. AI allows for bigger scope, it doesn't replace taste, vision and judgement.

replies.author: Plus_Combination_553
replies.body: "Scope" is a good word for it. AI lets me try three versions of a mechanic in one evening instead of one, but deciding which one feels right is still entirely on me.

comments.author: FervantFlea
comments.body:
It's still an absolutely enormous amount of work to get anything with a soul, same as developing a few years ago by hand. People really underestimate this. Anything AI spits out for you, even following a detailed game design doc (which 90% of people here aren't starting with), is going to be painfully generic. Everything about the design/layout/gamefeel will be an aggregate of mediocrity, that's just the way it is.

To get something that feels handmade, you still have to painstakingly and obsessively redo, refine, scrap, and claw at every tiny little detail until you pull that genericness out of it and create something that is actually your vision and not AI's vision. That's my 2 cents. I've been working on a project for 6 months, with 3x Claude Max subscriptions utilizing 100% usage around the clock, and I'm not close to having something polished enough that I'm comfortable posting it here. Most of the projects you see here are still one-shots people are doing without that amount of effort behind it.

replies.author: Plus_Combination_553
replies.body: Agree on the design doc point. Lately I create mine by talking to the AI in voice mode. Just explaining the idea out loud gets me new ideas, because I have to put my vision into words. Then the doc is something I actually pushed against and not just the AI's average. And the "scrap and redo" part is real too.

replies.author: MintL1
replies.body: Are you using Claude for code only or are you generating assets too? What area would you say is the biggest token eater that you experience?

replies.author: FervantFlea
replies.body:
No assets at all, all of my assets are human made. The very few times I have went to AI for assets have been done with OpenAI's models. Prior to this project I had no experience with doing 3D work at all. I'd say some of the biggest token pits have been around physics, networking (and especially networking physics), and my process of creating world and location generators that can output fun and well-designed areas.

I probably would've saved an enormous amount of time if I had prior experience with all of those token black holes.

comments.author: Any-Gap-933
comments.body: I take an interesting approach that is wasteful but it helps with my vision. I have claude build out a loose vision of what I want and then I either ship it or change 100% of it depending on the experience and what I see. Most of the time the foundation is good and the last 25-50% needs rework. Doing this combined with your own unique ideas helps as AI can't think outside the box.

comments.author: MintL1
comments.body: I would say the soul gets lost easily when using ai because of the tiny, but many important decisions that ai takes for you without you noticing it. With that said you can as others say use ai as a tool to speed up progress but design everything yourself

replies.author: romansamurai
replies.body: If you playtest your games and review all the decisions you should be able to catch that. If you’re letting AI make decisions for you and write the lore and scripts and characters and AI then yeah. It’s not your game anymore. Maybe your idea. But vibe coding lets you become a game director to manage and direct everything from systems to lore and story to art to mechanics and fine tuning and balancing. None of that should be lost if you’re not being lazy and letting AI do everything doe you.

replies.author: MintL1
replies.body: I just say that you can easily fall in the trap where you feel like every decision has been made by you but in reality it is actually ai. So you need to be careful.

comments.author: dank_summers
comments.body:
You have to slow down, can't just have half idea and let ai fill in the rest. Need to really think about everything and how it all ties in and interacts.

Sometimes I'm struggling with what to do with an aspect and I will use AI ideas to like spark a brainstorm of what I want, but you really can't have it finish your thoughts

replies.author: romansamurai
replies.body:
>Have an idea and let AI fill in the rest. 

That’s what I think is happening. People have some small concept or cool idea of a character or overall theme and then they let LLM build everything else from start to finish based on their little idea. Of course it’s going to be soulless.

replies.author: Plus_Combination_553
replies.body: Same here. I treat AI suggestions like a brainstorm with a coworker who has no taste: lots of options, but I pick, rewrite and cut. The problem starts when you stop deciding and just accept the first thing it gives you.

comments.author: Gustave232
comments.body: If your game is good enough people will get over it. Good enough is in all aspects. So even if you only guide your AI, you still need to know exactly what to do.

comments.author: Tri8ar
comments.body:
Ironically, a vibecoded game can have 100% soul and then some, because almost nothing stops you anymore from making the game exactly the way you want it.

You don't have to compromise around whatever tools, assets or plugins are available, or blend your vision with other people's taste.

Now your taste can leave its fingerprint on everything, and that's unprecedented. We could see a lot of truly auteur games that simply wouldn't have been possible before.

replies.author: Plus_Combination_553
replies.body: That's the part I find most interesting too: the limit shifts from tools and assets to how clearly you know what you want. "Auteur games" is a great way to put it. The catch is that the taste has to actually be there, because the AI will happily build something average if you don't push back.

comments.author: Galethorne
comments.body: To be honest, it's true that "your own touch" will be missing from a 100% vibe coded game and it's the little something that makes some indie games so amazing. If you know about the developer you can feel the person reflected in the art style, in the music, in the writing style and in the whole structure of the game itself. With AI, those parts are hardly yours. I think it's still possible, to some degree, though. Your writing style is probably the best way to insert your own personality and I would never ship a game with AI generated text lines whatsoever or even an AI-generated story. They might work if story isn't a crucial part of your game, but otherwise, don't ask AI to do creative parts like that for you. I also draw everything I want in my game as really shitty concept art to be as clear as possible what I want. Then I spend hours to fight AI for that and go through hundreds of revisions until it is what I want. I think that is something that will be reflected in "your" work.

replies.author: romansamurai
replies.body:
>To be honest, it's true that "your own touch" will be missing from a 100% vibe coded game and it's the little something that makes some indie games so amazing. If you know about the developer you can feel the person reflected in the art style, in the music, in the writing style and in the whole structure of the game itself. With AI, those parts are hardly yours.

Not true at all. This is the thinking of someone who has never done any vibe coding.

People let AI handle everything from writing to creating characters and having no input is what you’re talking about.  That’s also the problem with games feeling like they have no soul. People don’t have a concrete idea. They don’t take the time to actually build the game destined and the game details. They just have a rough idea of what they envisioned and let LLM take the reigns and do everything for them

Someone who has input on every tiny little decision will absolutely have their own touch in the game. The last thing you mentioned. Is exactly what I do too. I fight AI on every tiny little detail so in the end it looks the way I envisioned it even if my art is rudimentary.

replies.author: Galethorne
replies.body: That's basically what I said and I'm working on a 100% vibe coded game right now.

replies.author: romansamurai
replies.body: I probably should have specified. Not true at all was only to the first sentence. The rest I agree with you completely. I’ll fix it.

replies.author: Galethorne
replies.body: The first sentence was meant in a general sense because if you leave everything to the AI, no part of it will be from you.

replies.author: romansamurai
replies.body: Yup. I agree with that. But 100% vibe coded doesn’t mean nothing is from you. Vibe coding means not checking code. You look at the result and iterate from there. You still improve and tweak and add and verify and change every detail. Vibe coding specifically is “coding”. You tell AI in plain language what you want and focus on results instead of reviewing code.

comments.author: romansamurai
comments.body: Why would vibe coding remove the soul?  It’s our art direction, story, systems. If it’s missing it’s soul then most likely you had LLM do everything for you. I bc luring create the story, characters and decide on all the art.

comments.author: hyperg8_games
comments.body: Dont ask: "Create me a GTA 6 clone in a fantasy setting!" but more like: "I have that game idea about stealing cars, doing drug deals, marrying any partner and all of that should be in a fantasy setting, attached you will find my Game Design Document that details how I imagine my features to work, implement the GDD.md" and the AI will help you build your game, a game that adheres to your standards and your vision. From there on its just how much effort you put into every task and action needed, like creating music, sounds, 2d/3d visuals etc.. AI can be a powerful tool at executing, but not at imagining a play-worthy game (aside from 1:1 copying which has no value)

comments.author: donkeykong917
comments.body: Every single app you are using now will have some form of AI code. Not just games.

comments.author: The4modes
comments.body:
I feel like games don't really get a soul until you add the animations and all the small satisfying stuff like sounds and game feel, and that usually takes a while. When people talk about AI slop it's usually games where nobody bothered with that part, the AI got it working and then it just shipped.

To me the soul comes from all the decisions you make, like what feels good, what you cut and what you spend way too long polishing. AI can write the code but it can't decide what your game should feel like, so if you put that care in I don't think most players will care how it was made.

So no, I don't think using AI makes a game less valuable. It lowers the barrier of entry a lot, but the bar for something to actually be good is still the same, if not higher, since there are way more games out there now and it's harder to stand out.

The scary part for me is if AI ever gets good enough to make those decisions by itself, because then we're not really needed in the loop anymore.

replies.author: Plus_Combination_553
replies.body: Fully agree on the polish part. The gap between "it works" and "it feels good" is made of small decisions: a sound, a short delay, something you cut. On your last point: as long as the AI proposes and you choose, you're still the one in the loop. The risk is only if people stop choosing. Which part of polish do you find hardest to get right, sounds or animations?

replies.author: The4modes
replies.body: Generally the sound, mostly because I myself am not that good at it. I have some prior knowledge about anmation and modelling 3d objects, that way I cam mostly guide it and it works but for sound I myself doesn't have the language or knowledge do actually use the tool.

comments.author: loopywolf
comments.body:
Are you designing it? Are you making all the design choices, or do you just go with whatever the AI throws in?  If it is your design, then I say it has a soul.

All art is 99% tech and 1% inspiration, even drawing and painting.

replies.author: Plus_Combination_553
replies.body: To answer your question: yes. The ideas and design decisions are mine. I work them out with AI, and I've set it up so it never decides on its own. It proposes, I choose, and I do the acceptance testing myself, so nothing ends up in the game that I haven't played and approved. The soul comes from the decisions, not from who typed the code.

replies.author: loopywolf
replies.body:
🤝 Welcome!

I only recently joined the vibecoding game world..  I have only toyed with AI in my game development before, e.g. using it help me debug problems, or to add a specific feature, but 2 weeks ago for shots n goggles, I asked AI to make entire game for me, and I went a bit mad.. asked for another and another and another.. Every day, every evening, every weekend, just game-development every hour that came.

What I really like about it is precisely the point I made to you.. It allows us to focus entirely on the role of designer.  What do you want it to be like?  No, no, this isn't giving the right feel / is veering away from the intent.  Suddenly, my game-development speed and powers have doubled or trebled, or more, and I am madly in love with it.

replies.author: Plus_Combination_553
replies.body: Thanks for the welcome! That "no, this isn't the right feel" loop is exactly what I enjoy about it too, the AI does the typing and I stay in the designer seat. Do you keep a written design doc so it stays on your intent, or do you steer it purely through feedback as you go?

comments.author: Guildbound
comments.body: Your directing your AI your not asking to create what it thinks or else you will generic towns like Heartvale(mine was named like this and I’ve seen a few) better to create your own every step of the way.

comments.author: revel911
comments.body:
How do you keep a game’s soul if you hire all contractors?

Games have no soul when no soul was out into the idea

comments.author: fighthonor
comments.body: Build in batches.  Set up a batch of things you want build in the game. Once built have ai give you a list of things to go check yourself. You are the only one that can make the game feel like it has a soul. You gotta verify every step of the way so it keeps your vision and the games identity. Is also important to set those goals before your start your project. Write your goals down what do you want the game to feel like and look like, etc.

replies.author: Plus_Combination_553
replies.body: Good point about writing goals down first. I do something similar: I plan a roadmap from the start, which features go into the game and in what order, and AI helps with the implementation. Having the order fixed makes it easier to check each step against the plan.

comments.author: Double_Suggestion385
comments.body: Wtf is a soul? Just keep building. If it's fun people will play.

replies.author: Plus_Combination_553
replies.body: Fair question, and "fun" is the right bar. For me the "soul" is just the care you can feel when you play: the small details, the polish, the fact that someone made deliberate choices. Players notice when a game was put together carefully, even if they can't say why.

replies.author: Double_Suggestion385
replies.body: Then take the time to do that when using AI. Move slow, be deliberate in your prompts

replies.author: acexprt
replies.body: It really just depends on on the type of game.

comments.author: flpcut
comments.body: Add context to your prompts.. why you want features to be implemented, How they interact with other systems, whats their general goal in the game itself.

comments.author: WhosLive
comments.body: Most players can't tell how the code was written, they notice whether the game has a point of view. The stuff that usually reads as soulless is generic art, default UI, and mechanics that don't connect to each other, and that happens with handmade games too. Worth writing a short doc of the feeling you want and 2 or 3 rules the game always follows, then checking every AI change against it. Also spend your own time on the parts players touch most, like game feel, timing, sound, and the first 30 seconds. The disappointment people voice is usually about low effort asset flips, so showing your design decisions and iteration goes a long way.

comments.author: Felicitous_Mendacity
comments.body:
It came from you dude, it literally came out of your brain, it is 100% human generated. You approve and disapprove every decision that is made about your game. Did you code it, no, but you told it your vision and if it matches your vision that's human.

Now, if you went in and sais, make me a mobile game to make money and then uploaded it, yeah fuck that, that's lame as fuck.

replies.author: Plus_Combination_553
replies.body: Exactly, that's the line I draw too. The difference is whether someone cares about the result or just wants to ship something. I design the game, decide what goes in and what gets cut, and play-test everything myself, the AI just does the typing.

comments.author: acexprt
comments.body: For me, I’m trying to keep it a passion project, I’ve created games where I’ve had Claude do a lot of the story telling where I was pretty much not involved in a script, I used to do this intentionally so that I can play through the game and not know what’s coming. With my current game which is multiplayer Ive come to the same cross roads where I want to add some lore and story but I don’t know what, and I don’t want to hand that over to Claude this time. Ive decided to wait it out till I can sort through and plan it all out. The last thing you want is for a player to have that “oh this is AI” moment.  Keep your soul in the game and let the AI code it.

replies.author: Plus_Combination_553
replies.body: That "oh, this is AI" moment is a good thing to watch out for. I handle it the same way: story, lore and design decisions stay with me, and the AI helps with implementation. Waiting until you've planned the lore yourself sounds like the right call, because the story is the part players remember.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Build feature by feature, system by system, directly overseeing (and/or making, preferably) every asset that goes in the game. Really depends on how much effort you're putting into it.

When you tell AI, "I want to build a first person shooter"... It just gives you the boilerplate FPS shooter that has been overfitted to it in training so your game is identical to the thousands of others that asked for that same exact thing.

replies.author: Plus_Combination_553
replies.body: That's the overfitting problem in a nutshell. A vague prompt gets you the average of every game in that genre. What helps me is planning the feature order up front and starting from one mechanic that isn't standard for the genre. The more specific the idea, the less generic the output, and I check every step myself before the next feature goes in.

comments.author: TheHabeo
comments.body: you need consistent and coherent plan, originality in term of story, mechanics and concept of characters and the world. If you make the AI think for you, the game is not yours, its the AI's slopped up mess.
